items.title: Evaluating AI-assisted detection of fetal intracranial malformations in prenatal ultrasound practice: a multicentre, self-crossover, randomised controlled trial in China.
items.body: BACKGROUND: The effect of AI-assisted diagnosis on sonographer performance in real-world prenatal settings remains unclear. This study aimed to assess the Prenatal Ultrasound Diagnosis Artificial Intelligence Conduct System (PAICS) in detecting AI-recognisable intracranial malformations and its effect on identifying anomalies beyond its recognition scope in high-risk pregnancies. METHODS: This multicentre, self-crossover, randomised controlled trial was done at five Chinese centres. High risk of fetal malformation singleton pregnancies (11-32 weeks' gestation) were examined by sonographers with 3 to less than 8 years of experience. Participants were randomly assigned 1:1 to two diagnostic sequences: independent real-time diagnosis followed by PAICS-assisted offline review, or PAICS-assisted real-time diagnosis followed by independent offline review, with a 4-week washout period. Allocation was concealed. An expert panel's diagnosis on video review served as the reference standard. Sonographers were masked to fetal anomaly status but were aware of AI assistance during scanning. Outcome assessors and the independent expert panel responsible for the reference standard diagnosis were masked to group assignments. Primary outcomes were sensitivity and specificity in detecting ten specific fetal intracranial malformations, with sensitivity assessed for superiority and specificity against a 5% margin of non-inferiority. The trial is registered with the Chinese Clinical Trial Registry (ChiCTR2200063424). FINDINGS: Between Sept 6, 2022 and Nov 1, 2023, 1584 scans were completed. PAICS-assisted diagnosis improved sensitivity for detecting specific fetal intracranial malformations. In the fetal-based analysis, sensitivity increased by 0·087 (95% CI 0·029 to 0·147; p<0·0001), with specificity meeting the non-inferiority criterion (difference 0·009, 95% CI -0·006 to 0·023; p<0·0001). In the malformation-targeted analysis, sensitivity improved by 0·118 (95% CI 0·054 to 0·181; p<0·0001), and specificity was also non-inferior (difference 0·001, 95% CI -0·001 to 0·002; p<0·0001). No adverse events related to the diagnostic procedure or the AI assistance were reported. INTERPRETATION: PAICS improves sonographers' sensitivity for detecting targeted fetal intracranial malformations while preserving their specificity, which supports the integration of AI assistance into fetal anomaly screening in high-risk clinical settings. FUNDING: National Natural Science Foundation of China, Guangdong Provincial Basic and Applied Basic Research Fund Project, Guangzhou Science and Technology Program, and Sun Yat-sen University Fundamental Research Funds for the Junior Faculty Program.
items.why: This multicentre, self-crossover randomised controlled trial (RCT) in China tested an AI system (PAICS) for detecting ten fetal intracranial malformations in 1584 prenatal ultrasound scans, finding a significant sensitivity increase of 8.7 to 11.8 percentage points with specificity meeting non-inferiority criteria. This is a rare prospective, crossover-design clinical trial of AI-assisted fetal anomaly screening with a masked reference standard, giving it real weight for changing prenatal screening practice.
items.plain: Doctors in China tested an AI tool that helps ultrasound technicians spot brain abnormalities in fetuses, comparing the same doctors working with and without the AI's help across nearly 1600 scans. The AI helped them catch more real abnormalities without causing more false alarms, which is a strong, well-designed test that could support wider use of such tools in pregnancy screening.

items.title: Evaluating Frontline Health Workers' Responses to Patient Inquiries With and Without Large Language Model Support in Nigeria: Observational Study.
items.body: BACKGROUND: Frontline health workers (FLWs) in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs) often face barriers that compromise care quality, including limited training, high patient loads, inadequate access to updated clinical guidance, and resource constraints. Working in underserved settings further exacerbates challenges to providing accurate, complete, and empathetic responses. Addressing these gaps requires innovative tools to support FLWs in real time. OBJECTIVE: This study aims to evaluate the effectiveness of ChatGPT-3.5 in enhancing the quality of FLWs' responses to health inquiries in Lagos, Nigeria. METHODS: In this observational study, 36 licensed FLWs (doctors, nurses, community health workers) practicing general or primary care in Lagos, Nigeria, generated responses to 15 patient-generated health questions covering maternal and neonatal health, family planning, and sexually transmitted infections. Each FLW produced responses using their own knowledge and available resources ("human-only") and with ChatGPT-3.5 assistance ("GPT-aided"). A panel of 4 clinicians evaluated responses using a 5-point Likert scale for accuracy, empathy, contextualization, completeness, safety, and overall preference. In addition, 8 non-clinician health seekers assessed a subset of responses across 3 themes: Caring, Trust, and Ease of Understanding. RESULTS: Across 1080 responses from 36 FLWs, GPT-aided responses significantly outperformed human-only responses on all clinician-rated metrics (P<.001), with the largest gains observed in completeness, empathy, and overall preference, particularly among Community Health Extension Workers (CHEWs). Non-clinician evaluators also favored GPT-aided responses across all themes, with a strong preference for trust. CONCLUSIONS: This study provides empirical evidence that a large language model (ChatGPT-3.5) enhances the completeness, empathy, and perceived trust of responses by frontline health workers in Lagos, Nigeria. These findings underscore the potential of integrating ChatGPT-3.5 to strengthen healthcare delivery in resource-limited settings, highlighting the necessity for capacity building and further investigation into its safe, equitable, and effective implementation.
items.why: This observational study compared frontline health worker responses to patient questions on maternal, neonatal, and sexually transmitted infection topics in Lagos, Nigeria, with and without ChatGPT-3.5 assistance, finding large language model (LLM)-aided responses significantly outperformed human-only responses on clinician-rated accuracy, empathy, completeness, and safety across 1,080 responses from 36 workers. This is a genuine comparison against real health worker performance in a low-resource, high-stakes setting relevant to reproductive and maternal health, meeting this reader's bar for beat four evidence beyond routine chatbot scoring.
items.plain: In Nigeria, health workers answered real patient questions about pregnancy, newborn care, family planning, and sexually transmitted infections both on their own and with help from ChatGPT. When they used the AI, their answers were rated as noticeably more accurate, complete, caring, and safe by both doctors and everyday patients, showing real potential for AI to help overstretched health workers in under-resourced settings.

items.title: Effectiveness, Safety, and Workflow Burden of Large Language Model-Based Medical Report Generation: Systematic Review.
items.body: BACKGROUND: Systems based on large language models (LLMs), multimodal LLMs, and vision-language foundation models are increasingly being evaluated for medical report generation in imaging and related clinical workflows. Existing reviews have summarized technical architectures, radiology applications, readability, and benchmark performance, but clinical readiness remains uncertain because safety, human oversight, and workflow outcomes are sparsely and inconsistently reported. OBJECTIVE: The aim of this study is to assess the effectiveness (expert acceptance and blinded preference), safety (clinically significant, omission, and commission errors), and workflow burden (reporting time, corrections, edit distance, and editing burden) of LLM-based medical report generation. METHODS: We searched PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, Web of Science Core Collection, Scopus, and the Cochrane Library for studies published from January 1, 2016, through May 15, 2026. Eligible studies evaluated LLMs, multimodal LLMs, or vision-language foundation models for image-to-report generation, impression generation from findings, report drafting, or structured reporting in imaging workflows. Two reviewers performed screening, extraction, risk-of-bias assessment, and Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development, and Evaluation-informed narrative certainty assessment. Outcomes were clinically significant error rate, omission error rate, commission error rate, reporting time, edit burden, expert acceptance, and blinded expert preference. Meta-analysis was not performed because no comparable outcome had at least 2 studies with compatible task structure and analyzable data. RESULTS: A total of 101 studies were included. Chest x-ray was the largest modality group (36 studies), followed by computed tomography, magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), ultrasound, endoscopy, pathology, ophthalmic, electrocardiographic, dental, and mixed-modality contexts. No study was judged at low risk of bias; 15 were moderate, 72 high, and 14 serious. Safety and workflow evidence remained heterogeneous and largely nonpoolable. In a chest x-ray study, AI report acceptance was similar to that of radiologist reports (6047/8580, 70.5% vs 6288/8580, 73.3%), but false-negative findings were slightly higher (1584/8580, 18.5% vs 1527/8580, 17.8%). In a clinician-collaboration chest x-ray study, AI reports were equivalent or preferred in 233 of 300 (77.7%) and 170 of 303 (56.1%) cases across 2 datasets; yet, clinically significant errors persisted. In a brain MRI study, AI assistance reduced reading time from 61 to 53 seconds, whereas impression drafting increased editing time and edit distance. CONCLUSIONS: This review shifts the synthesis from plausible report generation to clinically interpretable effectiveness, safety, and workflow effects. Expert acceptance and preference suggested assistive value in selected supervised settings, but these signals were limited by inconsistent reporting of clinically significant errors, omissions, commissions, and failed generations. Workflow effects were mixed, with some studies reporting shorter reading time or drafting support, and others reporting greater editing time or edit distance. The evidence remains too heterogeneous, biased, and sparse on case-level end points to support a pooled meta-analysis or autonomous clinical-readiness claims. Adoption should remain locally validated, clinician-supervised, and accompanied by standardized reporting of acceptance, preference, omissions, commissions, failed generations, reporting time, corrections, and editing burden.
items.why: This systematic review synthesized 101 studies evaluating large language model (LLM)-based and vision-language foundation model medical report generation across imaging modalities, reporting expert acceptance, clinically significant error rates, and workflow burden, with example findings like near-equivalent acceptance to radiologist reports (70.5% vs 73.3%) but slightly higher false-negative rates. The review's strength is its scale and its explicit focus on safety and workflow outcomes rather than accuracy benchmarks alone, though the authors note universally elevated risk of bias and inability to pool most outcomes quantitatively, tempering the strength of its conclusions.
items.plain: This is a large review pulling together 101 studies that tested AI systems writing medical imaging reports, like chest X-ray summaries, and asking whether doctors accepted the AI's reports, how often it made errors, and how much extra work it created. The AI reports were about as often accepted as human radiologist reports but had a slightly higher rate of missed findings, and the review found that most individual studies had significant quality problems, so the overall picture remains uncertain.

items.title: Comparison of physician-authored and artificial intelligence-generated after-visit summaries: A blinded comparative study.
items.body: BACKGROUND: After-visit summaries (AVSs) are essential for a safe hospital discharge, yet are often written above literacy levels, omit key information, and are produced under substantial clinical time pressure. Large language models (LLMs) offer a potential solution, while performance and safety in real clinical workflows remain uncertain. OBJECTIVE: To compare the quality, understandability, actionability, and safety of LLM-generated versus physician-authored after-visit summaries for hospitalized patients. METHODS: We conducted a retrospective, blinded comparison of physician-authored AVSs and LLM-generated AVSs for 50 adults discharged from the University of California San Diego Health hospital medicine service in 2023. The physician-authored hospital course served as source text for generating AVSs using GPT-4 and Gemma 3n 2. Both were prompted to produce sixth-grade level, patient-centered AVSs. Five attending physicians independently evaluated each AVS using the Patient Education Materials Assessment Tool (PEMAT) for understandability and actionability and the AVSrubric, an instrument assessing accuracy, comprehensiveness, clarity, consistency with the medical record, tone and empathy, and potential for harm. RESULTS: LLM-generated AVSs had higher PEMAT scores than physician-authored AVSs (understandability: 85.5% (GPT-4), 87.5% (Gemma), and 66.1% (physician-authored); actionability: 70.9% (GPT-4), 74.1% (Gemma) vs. 56.7% (physician-authored); all p < .001). On the AVSrubric, LLM-generated AVSs received higher ratings than physician-authored AVSs across all domains with GPT-4 demonstrating significantly higher in all five, while Gemma showed significant improvements in clarity, readability, tone, and empathy. CONCLUSIONS: In this blinded evaluation, LLM-generated AVSs were clearer, more comprehensive, and more empathetic than physician-authored AVSs and were associated with lower physician-rated potential for harm. A physician-in-the-loop LLM workflow may improve discharge communication while reducing clinician burden and warrants prospective evaluation.
items.why: Blinded retrospective comparison of physician-authored versus large language model (LLM)-generated after-visit summaries for 50 hospitalized patients, rated by five attending physicians using the Patient Education Materials Assessment Tool (PEMAT) and a dedicated safety rubric, found LLM-generated summaries scored higher on understandability, actionability, and every quality domain, including lower perceived potential for harm. This is a real clinician-comparator study with a concrete, workflow-relevant document type and a harm-related outcome, making it one of the stronger entries this week for this beat despite its retrospective, single-center design.
items.plain: Doctors compared after-visit summaries written by human physicians against ones generated by AI for 50 hospital patients, with other doctors blindly judging both for clarity and safety. The AI-written summaries were rated clearer, more complete, more empathetic, and even safer than the human-written ones, suggesting AI could help with a task doctors often rush through, though this was a retrospective test at one hospital.

items.title: PREDICT-GBM: A multicenter platform advancing personalized glioblastoma radiotherapy planning.
items.body: Glioblastoma recurrence is largely driven by diffuse infiltration beyond radiologically visible margins, yet current radiotherapy guidelines rely on uniform margin expansions that ignore patient-specific biology and anatomy. While computational models promise to map this invisible growth and guide personalized planning, their clinical translation is hindered by a lack of standardized benchmarking and reproducible validation. To bridge this gap, we present PREDICT-GBM, an open-source platform integrating a curated, longitudinal, multi-center dataset of 243 patients with a standardized evaluation pipeline. We benchmark a novel U-Net-based recurrence prediction model against state-of-the-art biophysical and data-driven methods. Under iso-volumetric constraints, both biophysical and deep-learning approaches achieved modest but statistically significant gains in geometric coverage of future recurrence over guideline-based plans. On the combined cohort, our U-Net achieved the highest mean coverage of enhancing recurrence (79.37 ± 2.08%), surpassing guideline-based plans (paired Wilcoxon signed-rank test, Benjamini-Hochberg adjusted p = 2.9 × 10). The biophysical model GliODIL reached 78.91 ± 2.08% (p = 1.0 × 10), validating the platform's ability to compare diverse modeling paradigms. By providing a reproducible ecosystem for model training and validation, PREDICT-GBM addresses a major bottleneck toward personalized, computationally guided radiotherapy. The platform, models, and data are openly available at github.com/BrainLesion/PredictGBM .
items.why: PREDICT-GBM is an open-source, multicenter platform of 243 glioblastoma patients that benchmarks a new U-Net deep learning model against biophysical models for predicting tumor recurrence beyond visible margins, finding modest but statistically significant improvements in recurrence coverage over standard radiotherapy margins. The value here is mainly infrastructural, a reproducible benchmarking ecosystem, rather than a practice-changing clinical result, since gains were small and not yet tied to outcome data.
items.plain: Researchers built a shared, open dataset and testing platform from 243 brain cancer patients to compare different computer models that try to predict where a tumor will grow back after treatment, so doctors can plan radiation more precisely. Their best AI model slightly beat both standard guidelines and older prediction methods at covering future tumor regrowth, but the improvement was small and hasn't yet been shown to help patients live longer or have fewer side effects.

items.title: Deep learning-based automated cervical length measurement improves spontaneous preterm birth risk stratification in women with a borderline short cervix (20-25 mm) at mid-trimester: A retrospective cohort study.
items.body: OBJECTIVE: This study evaluates whether deep learning (DL)-based automated cervical length (CL) measurement provides improved risk stratification for spontaneous preterm birth (PTB), compared with conventional CL measurement methods, in women with a borderline short cervix by conventional methods (CL 20-25 mm) on mid-trimester ultrasound. METHODS: This retrospective cohort study was conducted in a tertiary referral hospital in South Korea between January 2019 and December 2023. Women with a conventionally measured borderline short cervix were reanalyzed using a previously validated DL-based algorithm (CL-Net) that traces the cervical canal, and were reclassified as DL-Normal (DL-CL > 25 mm) and DL-Short (DL-CL ≤ 25 mm) groups. The primary outcome was the risk of PTB before 37 weeks of gestation. Discrimination of conventional and DL-based CL was compared using receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curves with the DeLong test, and the incremental value of DL-based measurement was assessed by reclassification analyses. RESULTS: Of 171 women, 39 (22.8%) were reclassified into a DL-Short and 132 (77.2%) into a DL-Normal group. PTB before 37 weeks occurred in 28.2% of the DL-Short group and 6.1% of the DL-Normal group (P < 0.01), and a DL-Short cervix was independently associated with PTB (adjusted odds ratio, 6.37; 95% confidence interval, 2.28-17.84). DL-based CL showed better discrimination than conventional CL (area under the curve, 0.70 vs. 0.59; DeLong P = 0.042), with no evidence of poor calibration (Hosmer-Lemeshow, P = 0.36). The DL-Short group had a higher PTB rate despite greater progesterone use. For a DL-based CL ≤ 25 mm, sensitivity, specificity, positive predictive value, and negative predictive value for PTB were 57.9%, 81.6%, 28.2%, and 93.9%, respectively. CONCLUSION: Deep learning-based CL assessment, which follows the true anatomical pathway of the cervical canal, provides an objective and reproducible way to refine PTB risk stratification in women with a borderline short cervix. By identifying women at high risk of PTB more precisely than conventional methods, this approach could inform clinical practice, potentially helping to avoid unnecessary interventions in lower-risk women while ensuring appropriate preventive care for at risk patients with a borderline short cervix.
items.why: This retrospective cohort of 171 women with borderline short cervix (20-25 mm) found that a deep learning-based automated cervical length measurement tool improved discrimination of spontaneous preterm birth risk over conventional measurement (area under the curve 0.70 vs 0.59, DeLong p=0.042), with good calibration and a meaningful positive predictive value gain. The single-center, retrospective design and modest sample limit generalizability, but the improved risk stratification in an ambiguous clinical zone is clinically relevant for reproductive medicine.
items.plain: Doctors tested whether an AI tool that automatically measures cervix length could better predict premature birth risk than the usual manual measurement, focusing on 171 women whose cervix length fell in a borderline zone. The AI-based measurement identified high-risk women more accurately than the standard method, though the study was done at only one hospital and with a relatively small group of patients.

items.title: Abdominal landmark detection and classification of fetal growth conditions on obstetric ultrasound: a gestational age-conditioned multi-task network.
items.body: OBJECTIVE: This study presents GA-MTNet (Gestational-Age-Conditioned Multi-Task Network), a deep learning framework that integrates gestational age conditioning into a multi-task architecture to simultaneously perform abdominal landmark detection and classify five sonographic patterns linked to fetal growth conditions in prenatal ultrasound. MATERIALS AND METHODS: A retrospective multi-center dataset of 9,046 B-mode ultrasound images from 2,712 pregnant women (18-34 weeks) was collected across three institutions. Data from Centers A and B (6,750 images, 2,278 patients) were used for model development via patient-stratified 5-fold cross-validation, while Center C (1,296 images, 434 patients) served as an external test set. GA-MTNet employs a Swin Transformer V1 backbone with a Gestational Age Embedding Module based on Feature-wise Linear Modulation (FiLM), enabling dynamic adaptation of image features to fetal developmental stage. Three task heads handle: (1) detection of four abdominal landmarks, (2) five-class classification of fetal growth conditions (IUGR, GDM, pre-eclampsia, normal growth, amniotic fluid abnormalities), and (3) biometric regression. Post-deployment adaptability is supported through uncertainty-guided continual learning combining Monte Carlo Dropout, Elastic Weight Consolidation, and Low-Rank Adaptation. Interpretability was assessed via SHAP and Grad-CAM++, scored by two blinded fetal medicine specialists. RESULTS: Internally, GA-MTNet achieved a macro-AUC of 0.863, accuracy of 84.7%, macro-F1 of 0.821, and landmark detection mAP@0.5 of 0.791. Externally, performance remained strong (AUC 0.841, accuracy 82.3%, F1 0.798), with only a 2.2-point AUC drop. Per-class AUC ranged from 0.803 to 0.921. Ablation studies confirmed significant contributions from gestational age conditioning (+ 3.1 pp, p = 0.003), multi-task learning (+ 1.0 pp, p = 0.011), and continual learning (+ 1.0 pp, p = 0.014). Calibration was excellent (ECE = 0.047), and clinical relevance scored 3.2/4. CONCLUSIONS: GA-MTNet demonstrates that gestational age conditioning meaningfully improves sonographic pattern recognition and landmark detection across the second and third trimesters, while its continual learning mechanism enables safe, practical post-deployment model refinement.
items.why: This retrospective multi-center study developed GA-MTNet, a gestational age-conditioned multi-task deep learning model for abdominal landmark detection and classification of five fetal growth conditions on obstetric ultrasound, trained on 2712 patients and externally tested on an independent center with only a 2.2-point area under the curve (AUC) drop (0.863 internal vs 0.841 external). The external validation across institutions and detailed ablation analysis strengthen confidence in generalizability, though it remains a retrospective image-classification study without prospective clinical deployment data.
items.plain: Researchers built an AI system that looks at ultrasound images of a fetus's belly and simultaneously identifies key landmarks and flags signs of growth problems like restricted growth, gestational diabetes effects, or preeclampsia-related changes, adjusting its analysis based on how far along the pregnancy is. When tested on ultrasound images from a hospital it had never seen before, the AI's accuracy dropped only slightly, which is a good sign that it might work well in new hospitals too, though it has not yet been tested in real-time clinical use.

items.title: "Small" Large Language Models in the Hospital: Evaluation Study on Real-World Data in a Resource-Constrained Setting.
items.body: BACKGROUND: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly being deployed in health care, but their use and deployment in many real-world hospital environments pose significant challenges and concerns. In particular, state-of-the-art commercial models store or process data externally, which is often in conflict with ensuring patient data protection. At the same time, using LLMs locally is limited by the lack of available computing infrastructure. Small open-source LLMs that do not require substantial computing resources could offer a practical way to resolve these tensions, but their medical utility in real-world local contexts, especially in non-English languages, has not been sufficiently evaluated. OBJECTIVE: This study aimed to evaluate the feasibility of small, locally deployable open-source LLMs for clinically relevant tasks in a resource-constrained hospital setting and to propose a reproducible framework for institution-specific evaluation before deployment. METHODS: We evaluated 6 open-source LLMs ranging from 8B to 24B parameters (from the Mistral, Phi4, Falcon3, Llama3.1, and Meditron3 families) in a zero-shot setting across 7 tasks covering 4 clinical use cases: information extraction, medical text translation, text generation, and clinical decision support. We used deidentified French clinical data from a Swiss tertiary hospital, including discharge letters, clinical notes, and structured electronic health records. Performance was assessed using task-specific metrics, such as precision, recall, F-score, embedding-based semantic similarity, recall-oriented understudy for gisting evaluation (ROUGE) score, readability indices, and human review by clinicians. RESULTS: Model performance varied substantially between tasks. In the simplest retrieval task (needle-in-the-haystack), several models performed strongly, with Llama3.1 achieving an F-score of 99.81% and Mistral-small achieving 99.71%. In contrast, performance was poor in more complex tasks. For detecting protected health information, the best-performing LLMs achieved only modest overall macro-F-scores (0.33-0.34), substantially below a fine-tuned Robustly Optimized BERT Pretraining Approach (RoBERTa) baseline (0.94). In the task of extracting immune-related adverse events from discharge notes, the highest overall macro-F-score was 0.35 with Phi4. For medical text translation, Phi4 ranked highest in embedding-based evaluation, whereas Meditron3-Phi4 performed the worst, with clinician reviews identifying hallucinations in 55% of its outputs. In the task of summarizing discharge letters, quality was low across all models, with the best penalized ROUGE score reaching only 0.169 with Llama3.1. In the tasks of generating patient-friendly discharge note summaries and clinical decision support, clinician ratings generally ranged from dissatisfied to neutral, and no model achieved consistently satisfactory performance. CONCLUSIONS: Small open-source LLMs appear feasible for simple retrieval-oriented tasks in local hospital deployments but are currently inadequate for more complex applications, such as clinical decision support, deidentification, extraction of adverse events, and medical summarization. These findings highlight the importance of locally grounded evaluation tailored to specific use cases and the need for robust institutional evaluation frameworks to ensure safe and reliable deployment.
items.why: Evaluation of six open-source large language models (LLMs, 8 to 24 billion parameters) run locally on deidentified real French-language hospital data across four clinical tasks, finding strong performance on simple retrieval (F-scores near 99%) but poor performance on protected health information detection and adverse event extraction (macro-F-scores of 0.33 to 0.35), well below a fine-tuned Robustly Optimized BERT Pretraining Approach (RoBERTa) baseline. This is a real-world, deployment-oriented evaluation on live hospital data rather than a synthetic benchmark, which is unusually substantive for this beat even though it centers on clinical tasks rather than direct patient messaging.
items.plain: Researchers tested six smaller, privacy-friendly AI language models that could run inside a hospital's own computers, checking how well they handled real (anonymized) patient records for tasks like finding information and translating notes. The models did great at simple lookups but did poorly at harder jobs like spotting private information or dangerous drug reactions, doing much worse than an older but specially trained system built just for that job.

items.title: Generative artificial intelligence to augment ethical problem solving in ophthalmology: GPT-5.1 versus a human ethicist.
items.body: PURPOSE: While many large language models (LLMs) have been extensively investigated for their clinical decision-making capabilities, few studies have characterized their abilities to reason through complex, open-ended ethics cases. This study compared GPT-5.1 and expert human ethicist responses to real-world ethical scenarios specific to ophthalmology. METHODS: Ten ethical scenarios from the American Academy of Ophthalmology's Ask the Ethicist website were randomly selected and presented to GPT-5.1 using ChatGPT. AI-generated responses were subsequently compared to those of the expert human ethicist using conventional readability metrics. A panel of 10 physicians independently rated all responses via 6-point and 5-point Likert scales for both outcomes of likelihood-of-use in their own careers and perceived patient impact, respectively. RESULTS: GPT-5.1 versus human ethicist responses differed significantly on Flesch Reading Ease (10.9 ± 9.6 vs. 25.4 ± 10.9, p = 0.002) and Gunning Fog Index (21.3 ± 1.9 vs. 19.5 ± 2.9, p = 0.037). For likelihood-of-use, median ratings were 4.1 [3.8-4.3] for human ethicist versus 5.0 [4.7-5.2] for GPT-5.1 responses (p = 0.013). Median ratings for perceived patient impact of human ethicist versus GPT-5.1 responses were 3.6 [3.3-3.7] versus 3.9 [3.8-4.4], p = 0.008. Inter-rater reliability was moderate for both outcomes and response sources (ICC [2, 10]: 0.56-0.69). CONCLUSIONS: Compared to human ethicist responses, GPT-5.1 responses demonstrated lower readability; however, GPT-5.1 responses received significantly higher ratings for both outcomes of likelihood-of-use and perceived patient impact, respectively. These results advocate for further explorations of GPT-5.1 and other LLMs as potentially useful tools for evaluating common bioethical challenges in ophthalmology.
items.why: Ten ophthalmology ethics scenarios were answered by both GPT-5.1 and a human expert ethicist, and ten physicians rated both sets of responses on likelihood-of-use and perceived patient impact; GPT-5.1 scored significantly higher on both outcomes despite lower readability (Flesch Reading Ease of 10.9 versus 25.4). This is a genuine head-to-head comparison against a real clinical expert rather than a rubric applied to the model alone, which is the kind of evidence this beat values, though the sample is small and the domain (ethics reasoning) is narrow.
items.plain: Researchers compared an AI chatbot's answers to tricky ethical dilemmas in eye care against answers from a real professional ethicist, and had doctors rate both. The AI's answers were rated more useful and more impactful for patients than the human expert's, even though they were harder to read, though the number of scenarios tested was small.

items.title: Half of U.S. hospitals lack maternity wards as Medicaid cuts loom: report
items.body: Nearly half of U.S. hospitals are now without obstetric services, according to a new report, and closures could worsen as Medicaid cuts threaten hospital finances.
items.why: A new report finds nearly half of U.S. hospitals now lack obstetric services, with further closures anticipated as Medicaid funding cuts strain hospital finances. items.title: Evaluating retrieval-augmented generation versus long-context input for clinical reasoning over electronic health records.
items.body: OBJECTIVE: To evaluate whether retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) can serve as an efficient alternative to long-context prompting for clinical reasoning over electronic health records (EHRs). MATERIALS AND METHODS: We defined 3 EHR-based tasks that are replicable across health systems and vary in reasoning complexity: (1) extracting imaging procedures (modality, date, and anatomic site), (2) generating timelines of therapeutic antibiotic use, and (3) identifying the key diagnoses for a hospitalization. Using real inpatient clinical notes from a US academic health system, we evaluated 3 large language models (GPT-5.4-mini, Mistral Medium 3, DeepSeek V3.1) with varying amounts of provided context, comparing targeted retrieval to using the most recent clinical notes. RESULTS: For Imaging Procedures, RAG strongly outperformed recent-note inputs and exceeded long-context performance (by 0.17-9.83 F1 across all models) using fewer than 8K tokens. Similar benefits were observed for Antibiotic Timelines, where <8K of retrieved tokens matched long-context recent-notes performance (between -3.26 and +3.24 Jaccard). Error analysis revealed that missing information in the clinical notes-often due to inter-hospital transfers-limited performance to some extent. However, performance on the Diagnosis Generation task remains largely static across methods and models. DISCUSSION: RAG demonstrated strong token efficiency across tasks, with the clearest and most consistent gains observed for imaging extraction and antibiotic timeline reconstruction. Diagnosis generation proved the most challenging task, suggesting ceiling effects imposed by documentation variability and evaluation constraints. CONCLUSION: Our results suggest that RAG remains a competitive and efficient approach for clinical tasks over large amounts of EHR, even as newer models become capable of handling increasingly longer amounts of text.
items.why: This J Am Med Inform Assoc (JAMIA) study compared retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) against long-context prompting across three large language models for extracting information from real inpatient electronic health record (EHR) notes, finding RAG matched or exceeded long-context performance using far fewer tokens for imaging and antibiotic timeline tasks, though diagnosis generation remained unsolved. It is a useful applied informatics comparison on real clinical text, but it evaluates extraction accuracy rather than patient-facing communication or clinician workflow impact.
items.plain: Researchers tested whether giving an AI system only the most relevant pieces of a patient's medical record works as well as giving it the entire record, using real hospital notes and three different AI language models. The selective approach worked just as well or better for pulling out imaging details and antibiotic history using much less text, but neither approach reliably identified the main diagnoses for a hospital stay.

items.title: Progressive increase in ascending aortic diameter across the menopausal transition: A longitudinal study using AI-based automated measurement from chest radiographs.
items.body: BACKGROUND: Despite the menopausal transition being a critical period of accelerating cardiovascular disease (CVD) risk, structural remodeling of the thoracic ascending aorta during this phase remains poorly characterized. MATERIALS AND METHODS: We analyzed 4427 Korean women who were premenopausal at baseline and underwent posteroanterior chest radiography. Maximum ascending aortic diameter was quantified using validated software based on deep learning. Menopausal stage was classified per STRAW+10 criteria. Linear mixed-effects models were used to examine longitudinal aortic changes across menopausal stages and effect modification among groups classified according to their PREVENT score for 10-year CVD risk. RESULTS: Mean age at baseline was 40.2 ± 3.9 years. Over a median follow-up of 7.3 years, age-adjusted maximum ascending aortic diameter increased across menopausal stages, from 2.901 cm in premenopause to 2.991 cm in postmenopause, remaining significant after multivariable adjustment. The association differed by PREVENT 10-year CVD risk (P < 0.001). Among women in the lower three quartiles (quartiles 1-3, ≤0.8%), a significant increment was observed only in late transition (β = 0.035 cm; 95% CI 0.009, 0.061), whereas among those in the top quartile (quartile 4, >0.8%), the diameter showed progressive increases across all stages, with the largest increment in postmenopause (β = 0.094 cm; 95% CI 0.076, 0.112). CONCLUSION: Ascending aortic diameter showed progressive increases across the menopausal transition after adjustment for age and traditional CVD risk factors, with PREVENT-stratified differences. A significant increment even among women in the lower three quartiles during late transition suggests that stage-related differences in ascending aortic diameter may be detectable before menopause onset.
items.why: This longitudinal study of 4427 Korean women used a validated deep learning tool to automatically measure ascending aortic diameter on chest radiographs, finding progressive increases across the menopausal transition that were steeper in women with higher cardiovascular risk scores. The AI here is a measurement tool rather than the focus of validation, but the finding links menopausal staging to structural cardiovascular change with a reasonably large longitudinal sample.
items.plain: Researchers used an AI program that automatically measures the size of the main heart artery on chest X-rays to track nearly 4500 women as they went through menopause, finding that this artery gradually widens during the transition, especially in women already at higher heart disease risk. The AI's role was mainly to make consistent measurements rather than to be the object of the study itself.

items.title: Large language models show high clinical safety but differences in completeness for reproductive counselling in women with inflammatory rheumatic and musculoskeletal diseases: a comparative expert evaluation.
items.body: Specialized pregnancy counselling improves maternal and infant outcomes in women with inflammatory rheumatic and musculoskeletal diseases (iRMDs). As such services are not universally available, large language models (LLMs) may increasingly serve as an accessible source of information for patients seeking guidance on family planning, pregnancy, and lactation. This highlights the need to evaluate this software in terms of their adequacy, accuracy and overall reliability. The aim of the analysis is to evaluate the possibility of using LLMs as reliable sources of information regarding female patients suffering from iRMD and going through the period of pregnancy. 54 questions were formulated, which concern the impact and general relationship between pregnancy and rheumatic diseases. The questions were given to four LLMs, ChatGPT, DeepSeek, Gemini and Grok, and the corresponding answers were obtained. The responses were rated across three clinical domains on a 5-point Likert scale (ranging from 1 = strongly disagree/very poor to 5 = strongly agree/excellent) by ten European rheumatology experts and with the help of appropriate statistical indicators calculated, the reliability of the LLMs was assessed. 2160 items were evaluated. All models demonstrated high performance in "Clinical Safety" (Means > 4.10). For "Clinical Accuracy", DeepSeek and ChatGPT scored highest (Median 4.40 for both). Significant deviations were observed in "Completeness and Relevance", where DeepSeek dominated (Mean 4.24, 95% CI 4.17-4.30) and Gemini showed the lowest performance (Mean 3.46, 95% CI 3.27-3.64). Inter-rater agreement was poor to slight (Fleiss' kappa range: -0.043 to 0.059) and moderate for ICC (range: 0.259 to 0.692). LLMs currently exhibit uniformly strong safety behaviors when providing medical information about family planning, pregnancy and lactation in iRMD. However, significant differences exist regarding completeness and relevance, where DeepSeek and ChatGPT are currently the most reliable and complete models for this domain. Furthermore, the variability in responses and low inter-rater agreement highlight that LLMs require further parameterization, are useful tools for routine care, but cannot replace expert medical judgment.
items.why: This comparative expert evaluation had ten European rheumatology experts rate answers from four large language models (LLMs), including ChatGPT and DeepSeek, on 54 pregnancy-related counselling questions for women with inflammatory rheumatic and musculoskeletal diseases (iRMDs), finding high clinical safety scores but notable variability in completeness and poor inter-rater agreement (Fleiss' kappa as low as -0.043). The multi-model comparison and specialist rating add some value over routine chatbot-answer studies, but the absence of a clinician-answer comparator and the low inter-rater reliability limit how much this changes practice.
items.plain: Researchers had ten rheumatology specialists grade the answers of four AI chatbots to 54 common questions pregnant patients with rheumatic diseases might ask, checking for safety, accuracy, and completeness. All the chatbots gave safe answers, but they varied in how complete their answers were, and the human experts often disagreed with each other about how good the answers were, which makes the ratings less trustworthy.

items.title: Sentence-Level Provenance for AI Medical Record Summarization in a Click-to-Inspect Interface: Formative Usability Evaluation.
items.body: BACKGROUND: Large language models can generate fluent summaries of longitudinal medical records, but in high-stakes clinical settings, verification burden remains a barrier to trust. Existing provenance mechanisms such as document-level citations and section references often require manual search within long, fragmented notes, limiting their usefulness during time-constrained workflows for clinicians. OBJECTIVE: This study aimed to design and evaluate a sentence-level provenance interface ("click to inspect") that enables rapid verification of AI-generated longitudinal medical record summaries at the level of individual statements. METHODS: Between November 2023 and January 2024, we conducted a formative usability study using remotely moderated usability sessions via Zoom to evaluate a web-based sentence-level provenance interface for AI-generated longitudinal medical record summaries. A convenience sample of clinicians was recruited through email outreach to academic and professional networks across the United States. Formative usability testing was conducted with 46 clinician interactions using synthetic longitudinal patient charts. Participants included medical students, residents, and attending physicians across multiple specialties, including internal medicine, dermatology, radiology, plastic surgery, anesthesiology, interventional radiology, obstetrics and gynecology, and family medicine. Usability was assessed using the System Usability Scale and net promoter score, alongside qualitative feedback. RESULTS: Clinicians reported high usability (mean System Usability Scale score 86.25, SD 7.77; 95% CI 83.96-88.54 from 46 participants) and a positive overall experience (net promoter score of 35; 22/46, 47.8% promoters; 18/46, 39.1% passives; and 6/46, 13% detractors). Participants described rapid access to supporting evidence as critical for trust calibration during first-pass chart review. Qualitative feedback identified friction in traditional citation-based interfaces and supported sentence-level inspectability as a low-friction verification mechanism. CONCLUSIONS: Sentence-level provenance transforms AI-generated summaries from static narratives into interactive verification tools. An approach that enables rapid, selective inspection of individual claims during longitudinal chart review may reduce verification burden and support calibrated reliance in high-risk clinical contexts.
items.why: This formative usability study evaluated a sentence-level provenance interface, letting clinicians click to verify individual claims in large language model (LLM)-generated longitudinal medical record summaries, with 46 clinicians reporting high System Usability Scale scores (mean 86.25) and a positive net promoter score. The design targets a real deployment barrier, verification burden, though the study is small, formative, and uses synthetic rather than real patient charts, so it does not yet demonstrate an effect on real-world clinical workflow or patient outcomes.
items.plain: Researchers built a tool that lets doctors click on any sentence in an AI-written patient summary to instantly see the original medical record it came from, making it easier to check if the AI got it right. In an early test with 46 clinicians using fake practice charts, they liked the tool a lot, but it has not yet been tested on real patients or real workloads.

scored.title: Evaluating AI-assisted detection of fetal intracranial malformations in prenatal ultrasound practice: a multicentre, self-crossover, randomised controlled trial in China.
scored.why: This multicentre, self-crossover randomised controlled trial (RCT) in China tested an AI system (PAICS) for detecting ten fetal intracranial malformations in 1584 prenatal ultrasound scans, finding a significant sensitivity increase of 8.7 to 11.8 percentage points with specificity meeting non-inferiority criteria. This is a rare prospective, crossover-design clinical trial of AI-assisted fetal anomaly screening with a masked reference standard, giving it real weight for changing prenatal screening practice.

scored.why: This multicentre, self-crossover randomised controlled trial (RCT) in China tested an AI system (PAICS) for detecting ten fetal intracranial malformations in 1584 prenatal ultrasound scans, finding a significant sensitivity increase of 8.7 to 11.8 percentage points with specificity meeting non-inferiority criteria. This is a rare prospective, crossover-design clinical trial of AI-assisted fetal anomaly screening with a masked reference standard, giving it real weight for changing prenatal screening practice.

scored.title: Evaluating Frontline Health Workers' Responses to Patient Inquiries With and Without Large Language Model Support in Nigeria: Observational Study.
scored.why: This observational study compared frontline health worker responses to patient questions on maternal, neonatal, and sexually transmitted infection topics in Lagos, Nigeria, with and without ChatGPT-3.5 assistance, finding large language model (LLM)-aided responses significantly outperformed human-only responses on clinician-rated accuracy, empathy, completeness, and safety across 1,080 responses from 36 workers. This is a genuine comparison against real health worker performance in a low-resource, high-stakes setting relevant to reproductive and maternal health, meeting this reader's bar for beat four evidence beyond routine chatbot scoring.

scored.title: Effectiveness, Safety, and Workflow Burden of Large Language Model-Based Medical Report Generation: Systematic Review.
scored.why: This systematic review synthesized 101 studies evaluating large language model (LLM)-based and vision-language foundation model medical report generation across imaging modalities, reporting expert acceptance, clinically significant error rates, and workflow burden, with example findings like near-equivalent acceptance to radiologist reports (70.5% vs 73.3%) but slightly higher false-negative rates. The review's strength is its scale and its explicit focus on safety and workflow outcomes rather than accuracy benchmarks alone, though the authors note universally elevated risk of bias and inability to pool most outcomes quantitatively, tempering the strength of its conclusions.

scored.title: Comparison of physician-authored and artificial intelligence-generated after-visit summaries: A blinded comparative study.
scored.why: Blinded retrospective comparison of physician-authored versus large language model (LLM)-generated after-visit summaries for 50 hospitalized patients, rated by five attending physicians using the Patient Education Materials Assessment Tool (PEMAT) and a dedicated safety rubric, found LLM-generated summaries scored higher on understandability, actionability, and every quality domain, including lower perceived potential for harm. This is a real clinician-comparator study with a concrete, workflow-relevant document type and a harm-related outcome, making it one of the stronger entries this week for this beat despite its retrospective, single-center design.

scored.title: PREDICT-GBM: A multicenter platform advancing personalized glioblastoma radiotherapy planning.
scored.why: PREDICT-GBM is an open-source, multicenter platform of 243 glioblastoma patients that benchmarks a new U-Net deep learning model against biophysical models for predicting tumor recurrence beyond visible margins, finding modest but statistically significant improvements in recurrence coverage over standard radiotherapy margins. The value here is mainly infrastructural, a reproducible benchmarking ecosystem, rather than a practice-changing clinical result, since gains were small and not yet tied to outcome data.

scored.title: Deep learning-based automated cervical length measurement improves spontaneous preterm birth risk stratification in women with a borderline short cervix (20-25 mm) at mid-trimester: A retrospective cohort study.
scored.why: This retrospective cohort of 171 women with borderline short cervix (20-25 mm) found that a deep learning-based automated cervical length measurement tool improved discrimination of spontaneous preterm birth risk over conventional measurement (area under the curve 0.70 vs 0.59, DeLong p=0.042), with good calibration and a meaningful positive predictive value gain. The single-center, retrospective design and modest sample limit generalizability, but the improved risk stratification in an ambiguous clinical zone is clinically relevant for reproductive medicine.

scored.title: Abdominal landmark detection and classification of fetal growth conditions on obstetric ultrasound: a gestational age-conditioned multi-task network.
scored.why: This retrospective multi-center study developed GA-MTNet, a gestational age-conditioned multi-task deep learning model for abdominal landmark detection and classification of five fetal growth conditions on obstetric ultrasound, trained on 2712 patients and externally tested on an independent center with only a 2.2-point area under the curve (AUC) drop (0.863 internal vs 0.841 external). The external validation across institutions and detailed ablation analysis strengthen confidence in generalizability, though it remains a retrospective image-classification study without prospective clinical deployment data.

scored.title: "Small" Large Language Models in the Hospital: Evaluation Study on Real-World Data in a Resource-Constrained Setting.
scored.why: Evaluation of six open-source large language models (LLMs, 8 to 24 billion parameters) run locally on deidentified real French-language hospital data across four clinical tasks, finding strong performance on simple retrieval (F-scores near 99%) but poor performance on protected health information detection and adverse event extraction (macro-F-scores of 0.33 to 0.35), well below a fine-tuned Robustly Optimized BERT Pretraining Approach (RoBERTa) baseline. This is a real-world, deployment-oriented evaluation on live hospital data rather than a synthetic benchmark, which is unusually substantive for this beat even though it centers on clinical tasks rather than direct patient messaging.

scored.title: Generative artificial intelligence to augment ethical problem solving in ophthalmology: GPT-5.1 versus a human ethicist.
scored.why: Ten ophthalmology ethics scenarios were answered by both GPT-5.1 and a human expert ethicist, and ten physicians rated both sets of responses on likelihood-of-use and perceived patient impact; GPT-5.1 scored significantly higher on both outcomes despite lower readability (Flesch Reading Ease of 10.9 versus 25.4). This is a genuine head-to-head comparison against a real clinical expert rather than a rubric applied to the model alone, which is the kind of evidence this beat values, though the sample is small and the domain (ethics reasoning) is narrow.

scored.title: Half of U.S. hospitals lack maternity wards as Medicaid cuts loom: report
scored.why: A new report finds nearly half of U.S. hospitals now lack obstetric services, with further closures anticipated as Medicaid funding cuts strain hospital finances. This is a concrete, system-level finding about access to maternity care rather than a single company's action, and it signals a structural shift the reader's field should track even without an AI component.

scored.title: Evaluating retrieval-augmented generation versus long-context input for clinical reasoning over electronic health records.
scored.why: This J Am Med Inform Assoc (JAMIA) study compared retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) against long-context prompting across three large language models for extracting information from real inpatient electronic health record (EHR) notes, finding RAG matched or exceeded long-context performance using far fewer tokens for imaging and antibiotic timeline tasks, though diagnosis generation remained unsolved. It is a useful applied informatics comparison on real clinical text, but it evaluates extraction accuracy rather than patient-facing communication or clinician workflow impact.

scored.title: Progressive increase in ascending aortic diameter across the menopausal transition: A longitudinal study using AI-based automated measurement from chest radiographs.
scored.why: This longitudinal study of 4427 Korean women used a validated deep learning tool to automatically measure ascending aortic diameter on chest radiographs, finding progressive increases across the menopausal transition that were steeper in women with higher cardiovascular risk scores. The AI here is a measurement tool rather than the focus of validation, but the finding links menopausal staging to structural cardiovascular change with a reasonably large longitudinal sample.

scored.title: Large language models show high clinical safety but differences in completeness for reproductive counselling in women with inflammatory rheumatic and musculoskeletal diseases: a comparative expert evaluation.
scored.why: This comparative expert evaluation had ten European rheumatology experts rate answers from four large language models (LLMs), including ChatGPT and DeepSeek, on 54 pregnancy-related counselling questions for women with inflammatory rheumatic and musculoskeletal diseases (iRMDs), finding high clinical safety scores but notable variability in completeness and poor inter-rater agreement (Fleiss' kappa as low as -0.043). The multi-model comparison and specialist rating add some value over routine chatbot-answer studies, but the absence of a clinician-answer comparator and the low inter-rater reliability limit how much this changes practice.

scored.title: Sentence-Level Provenance for AI Medical Record Summarization in a Click-to-Inspect Interface: Formative Usability Evaluation.
scored.why: This formative usability study evaluated a sentence-level provenance interface, letting clinicians click to verify individual claims in large language model (LLM)-generated longitudinal medical record summaries, with 46 clinicians reporting high System Usability Scale scores (mean 86.25) and a positive net promoter score. The design targets a real deployment barrier, verification burden, though the study is small, formative, and uses synthetic rather than real patient charts, so it does not yet demonstrate an effect on real-world clinical workflow or patient outcomes.

scored.title: Development and Usability Assessment of a Health Education Conversational Agent for Patients With Gastric Cancer: Action Research Study.
scored.why: Researchers deployed a retrieval-augmented generation (RAG)-based conversational agent for gastric cancer patient education at a Chinese cancer center, iteratively testing accuracy across three alpha rounds (rising from 67% to 82%) and assessing usability and experience among patients and staff. This is a real deployment with quantified accuracy and stakeholder feedback rather than a benchmark exercise, though it lacks a comparison against human-delivered education or measured patient outcome change, capping its impact for this reader's discriminating standard.

scored.title: An operational perturbation proteomics-based virtual cell model.
scored.why: This Nature paper describes ProteinTalks, a virtual cell model trained on over 38 million perturbation proteomics measurements from breast cancer cell lines, intended to predict drug efficacy, synergy, and resistance, with some transfer to patient-derived organoids and biopsies. It is an ambitious computational drug-discovery tool but remains preclinical, with no prospective clinical validation or trial data, limiting its immediate relevance to bedside care.

scored.title: Prospective accuracy study on an artificial intelligence-based ultrasound system for gestational age estimation among pregnant women in Ghana, Kenya and South Africa: protocol.
scored.why: This is a study protocol for a multicountry prospective cohort in Ghana, Kenya, and South Africa validating an AI-based handheld ultrasound system for gestational age estimation against crown-rump length, enrolling 969 women across 13 facilities. As a protocol with no results yet, it signals an important upcoming validation for low-resource obstetric AI but currently offers no findings to act on.

scored.title: A pilot study to implement artificial intelligence-enabled, point-of-care obstetric ultrasound for gestational age estimation in Zambia: An evaluation protocol.
scored.why: This is an evaluation protocol for a pilot program integrating AI-enabled point-of-care ultrasound (POCUS) for gestational age dating into routine antenatal care across six facilities in Zambia, using a mixed-methods implementation science framework. As a protocol, it describes planned feasibility and acceptability assessment rather than reporting actual accuracy or outcome data.

scored.title: Using Speech to Develop Multivariable Prediction Models for Major Depressive Disorder and Generalized Anxiety Disorder During Pregnancy.
scored.why: This small prediction model study used speech features from 146 pregnant women to build machine learning classifiers for major depressive disorder (MDD) and generalized anxiety disorder (GAD), reporting F1-scores of 74-80% for full-interview models but poor performance (42-45%) when restricted to patient-only verified speech segments. The modest sample size, lack of external validation, and no comparison to clinician diagnostic accuracy limit its immediate clinical relevance.

scored.title: Mouse oocyte phenotypes differ in blastocyst response to resveratrol and vitamin B12.
scored.why: This experimental study clustered mouse oocytes by radiomics-derived morphological features and found that blastocyst formation response to resveratrol or vitamin B12 supplementation differed by cluster and maternal age, with overall blastocyst formation rising from 37% to 56% when the best medium was matched to each cluster-age combination. The approach hints at a personalized culture-condition strategy for oocyte selection, but it is a small preclinical mouse study requiring prospective validation before any relevance to human in vitro fertilization (IVF) practice.

scored.title: A two-stage evaluation of large language models for guideline-based Q&A and draft rehabilitation planning in stroke care.
scored.why: Two-stage evaluation compared four large language models (LLMs) on stroke guideline question-answering, then had the top two, ChatGPT-o3 and DeepSeek, generate individualized rehabilitation plans for 60 deidentified cases rated by three clinicians on correctness, completeness, readability, helpfulness, and safety, with ChatGPT-o3 outperforming DeepSeek in plan generation. This is a single-center, model-versus-model benchmark without a real clinician-authored comparator or patient-facing deployment, so it is useful but not standout evidence for this beat.

scored.title: International qualitative case studies of system-level approaches to promote the development, adoption, and implementation of artificial intelligence in healthcare.
scored.why: This qualitative study interviewed 50 stakeholders across four health systems (Catalonia, Norway, Singapore, Queensland) about strategies for scaling AI adoption, identifying themes like digital infrastructure, governance, and post-deployment monitoring. It offers descriptive, cross-case thematic findings rather than measurable outcomes or generalizable evidence about AI performance or impact.

scored.title: Machine Learning and Functional Analysis of Placental DNA Methylation Signatures for Early-Onset Preeclampsia.
scored.why: This retrospective study used machine learning classifiers on placental DNA methylation beta-values from a modest cohort to distinguish early-onset preeclampsia (EOPE) from controls, reporting high cross-validated accuracy (95.45%) and area under the curve (AUC 0.9545) with an independent validation set. The very high accuracy in a small, likely homogeneous dataset without prospective or multi-site external validation raises concern about overfitting and limited generalizability.

scored.title: Association between high fat, sugar, and sodium diet and adverse pregnancy outcomes, modified by fruit and vegetable intake density.
scored.why: This study used a doubly robust machine learning estimator to test whether fruit and vegetable intake density modifies the association between a high fat, sugar, and sodium diet and adverse pregnancy outcomes in a prospective cohort of 8,259 nulliparous women. The finding was essentially null, with imprecise, wide confidence intervals, so it offers little actionable signal and the machine learning component is a statistical tool rather than a clinical AI application.

scored.title: Reconstructing signaling histories of single cells via perturbation screens and transfer learning.
scored.why: This Nature Methods paper describes IRIS, a neural network trained via transfer learning on a perturbation atlas of human pluripotent stem cells, then applied to infer signaling histories in mouse embryo single-cell atlases. It is a sophisticated basic-science methods contribution to developmental biology but has no direct clinical application to human reproductive or obstetric care, limiting its relevance to this reader's clinical AI beats.

scored.title: Causal adiposity and clinical validation of regional fat distribution in PMOS: a multi-modal analysis integrating GBD 2021, Mendelian randomization, and machine learning.
scored.why: This multi-modal study combined Global Burden of Disease (GBD) 2021 data, Mendelian randomization for causal inference, and an XGBoost machine learning model (area under the curve, AUC, of 0.701) to link regional fat distribution with polycystic ovary syndrome, now relabeled polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome (PMOS) in this paper. The causal genetic evidence is informative, but the clinical prediction model has only modest discriminative performance and lacks external validation, limiting its immediate clinical utility.

scored.title: Comparative quality, accuracy, and readability of large language model responses to patient questions about robotic-assisted total knee arthroplasty.
scored.why: This study compared four large language models (LLMs), including ChatGPT-o3, ChatGPT-5.2, Gemini 3, and DeepSeek, on quality, accuracy, and readability of answers to patient questions about robotic-assisted total knee arthroplasty, finding acceptable but variable accuracy and readability consistently above recommended patient education levels. Per this reader's standards, comparing chatbot outputs across models on rubric scores without a clinician comparator is a routine study design that adds little new insight.

scored.title: Tool or Companion? Reframing Conversational AI to Prevent Psychological Harm.
scored.why: This is a conceptual and opinion piece arguing that conversational artificial intelligence (AI) should be understood as a tool rather than a companion, discussing mechanisms like simulated empathy and sycophancy that may reinforce maladaptive beliefs in vulnerable users. It presents no new empirical data or clinical comparison, making it commentary rather than an evaluable study relevant to this reader's discriminating standard for beat four.

scored.title: Large Language Models for Breast Cancer Education: A Comparative Analysis of Quality, Reliability and Readability.
scored.why: Cross-sectional comparison of ChatGPT-5.3 and Gemini 3.0 Flash on 40 breast cancer questions, scored by three surgeons using modified DISCERN (mDISCERN) reliability and Global Quality Score (GQS) rubrics plus standard readability indices; Gemini scored higher on both quality and readability, but both models exceeded recommended sixth-grade reading level. This is a rubric-based model-versus-model comparison with no clinician-generated answers as a baseline, which the reader's beat treats as routine rather than novel.

scored.title: Stigma-sensitive communication in medical students: an AI-supported simulation of a patient living with HIV.
scored.why: Mixed-methods study of 260 Turkish medical students who conducted a text-based simulated patient interview with ChatGPT-4o role-playing a person living with HIV, rating student empathy and stigma-sensitive communication with only a weak correlation between self- and educator-assessment (r = 0.136). This uses a large language model (LLM) as a training tool rather than evaluating the LLM's own communication with real patients, so it is tangential to the beat's focus on model-patient interaction quality.

scored.title: Simultaneous ChatGPT-4o outputs for type 2 diabetes pharmacotherapy: Accuracy, usefulness, and impact variability.
scored.why: Five clinical pharmacists used a modified Delphi consensus process to rate accuracy and usefulness of ChatGPT-4o outputs generated simultaneously across three separate sessions for the same diabetes-related prompts, finding some variability in accuracy and usefulness between identical queries. This is a small, single-model consistency check without any comparison to real clinician-authored answers or patient outcomes, making it a modest addition to the literature.

scored.title: ChatGPT 4.o Responses to Commonly Asked Colon and Rectal Cancer Questions From a Patient Perspective.
scored.why: A five-surgeon panel rated ChatGPT-4o's answers to ten patient questions about colon and rectal cancer surgery on completeness, accuracy, and communication using 5-point Likert scales, with average scores around 13 out of 15. There is no comparator of real clinician-written answers or patient outcome measure, making this a routine rubric-scoring study for this beat.

scored.title: Health artificial intelligence is here, but are we measuring what matters?
scored.why: This is a perspective piece arguing that health AI evaluation should shift from technical validity metrics toward outcomes-based, systems-level assessment, contrasting deontological and consequentialist frameworks. It contains no new data or study, making it a commentary rather than evidence that should change practice.

scored.title: Integrative Transcriptomic and Network Pharmacology Analysis Suggests Potential Mechanisms of Propofol in Early-Onset Preeclampsia.
scored.why: This study used network pharmacology and machine learning feature selection (LASSO, support vector machine, Boruta) on small transcriptomic datasets to propose propofol targets in early-onset preeclampsia, validated with molecular docking and RT-qPCR in a 36-patient cohort. The machine learning component is a minor bioinformatics filtering step within a mechanistic wet-lab study, and it has no bearing on AI-based clinical prediction or care.

scored.title: Efficacy of icariin in polycystic ovary syndrome: Cathepsin S as a key target revealed by computational and experimental evidence.
scored.why: This study combined network pharmacology, an optimized machine learning framework across 113 algorithm combinations, and mouse experiments to propose Cathepsin S as a target for icariin's effect on polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS). The machine learning use is a target-selection step within a broader mechanistic pharmacology study, with no clinical prediction, patient data, or diagnostic application relevant to reproductive AI.

scored.title: Self-Reported Knowledge, Attitudes, Perceptions, and Readiness Regarding AI Among Obstetrics and Gynecology Trainees: Cross-Sectional Study.
scored.why: This cross-sectional survey of 218 obstetrics and gynecology (O&G) trainees in Jordan assessed self-reported knowledge, attitudes, and readiness regarding AI, finding moderate readiness and little formal AI training. It is a workforce attitudes survey with no AI performance data or patient impact, offering limited actionable insight for a clinical AI researcher.

scored.title: Artificial intelligence in reproductive medicine and education: current evidence, challenges, and future directions.
scored.why: This is a narrative review of the past decade of literature on AI in reproductive medicine education, covering large language models (LLMs), ultrasound training, and assessment tools, concluding AI should be a supervised educational adjunct rather than an autonomous substitute. As a review without new data, it summarizes existing concerns like hallucination risk but offers no new evidence to act on.

scored.title: The triple burden of malnutrition and the role of machine learning: A systematic review.
scored.why: This systematic review summarizes machine learning applications for predicting malnutrition across life stages, noting decision trees, random forests, and neural networks perform well but that research on pregnant women and adolescents remains limited. It is a broad review without new data or a specific reproductive AI application, and its relevance to reproductive endocrinology and infertility or obstetric AI is only tangential.

scored.title: Reassessing Semen Analysis: Clinical Insights Beyond Sperm Count and Motility.
scored.why: This is a narrative review summarizing conventional semen analysis alongside emerging biofunctional, omics, and artificial intelligence (AI)-assisted approaches to male infertility evaluation, without presenting new data or a systematic evidence synthesis. It is useful background reading but contains no findings that would change clinical practice or research priorities this week.

scored.title: Digital health nursing in male infertility: Leadership, workforce, and policy pathways for equitable care.
scored.why: This narrative review synthesizes literature from 2018 to 2025 on digital health tools, including artificial intelligence (AI), for male infertility care and proposes a leadership model for nurse-mediated implementation, but it contains no primary data or outcome evaluation. It is a policy and framework piece rather than an evidence-generating study.

scored.title: Integrative transcriptomic identification of potential common biomarkers between non-obstructive azoospermia and papillary thyroid cancer via multi-algorithmic machine learning and network biology approaches.
scored.why: This study used five machine learning algorithms on public transcriptomic datasets to identify shared biomarkers between non-obstructive azoospermia and papillary thyroid cancer, reporting area under the curve (AUC) values up to 0.95 in a purely retrospective, bioinformatic setting without prospective or external clinical validation. The work is exploratory molecular biology rather than a clinically actionable AI application.

scored.title: Integrative Transcriptomic Analysis and Functional Validation Implicate GPT2 in Glycolytic Regulation in Polycystic Ovary Syndrome.
scored.why: This study combined transcriptomic data mining, several machine learning algorithms for feature selection, and laboratory experiments in granulosa cells to implicate GPT2 in glycolytic dysfunction in polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS). The machine learning component is used only for variable prioritization within a molecular biology study, and the work does not offer a clinically actionable diagnostic or predictive tool.

scored.title: Wearable Sensors Offer Opportunities for Phenotyping Perinatal Mood Disorders: a Narrative Review.
scored.why: This is a narrative review proposing that wearable sensor data, combined with machine learning, could enable continuous phenotyping of perinatal mood disorders beyond periodic clinical assessments. No new data, cohort, or model performance is presented, making this a conceptual piece rather than evidence of a working approach.

scored.title: Exploring Bias in Medical Applications of Large Language Models: Protocol for a Systematic Review.
scored.why: This is a protocol for a systematic review evaluating how bias is detected, measured, and mitigated in medical applications of large language models (LLMs), including a plan to validate a large language model-assisted screening workflow against manual review. No results are yet available, as screening of the updated dataset is described as ongoing.

scored.title: The importance of response generation protocols in chatbot-based patient education studies.
scored.why: This item has no abstract text available, only a title suggesting a commentary on methodology standards for chatbot patient-education studies. Without content to assess, it cannot be judged for evidentiary value and is likely opinion rather than new data.

scored.title: Research priorities in Spine Deformity: a machine learning-based topic analysis of the journal's first decade (2013-2026).
scored.why: Applies BERTopic, a transformer-based topic-modeling method, to cluster 1851 abstracts from a scoliosis surgery journal and identify trending research themes over a decade, including a minor emerging cluster on LLM-based patient education. This is bibliometric analysis of a field's literature, not a study of an AI system's clinical performance or patient interaction, so it falls outside what this beat is meant to track.

scored.title: Closing the Solidarity Gap Requires Closing the Accountability Gap for Patient-Facing AI.
scored.why: This is an opinion commentary arguing that closing the accountability gap in patient-facing artificial intelligence (AI) requires shared governance among clinicians, developers, and payers, with no new data or study design presented. It restates a policy position already familiar to readers in this space rather than offering new evidence.

scored.title: Occurrence of triethylamine in water bodies of a chemical industrial park and its toxicological mechanisms on zebrafish embryo-larvae.
scored.why: This is an environmental toxicology study assessing triethylamine (TEA) contamination and its thyroid-disrupting effects in zebrafish embryos, with no artificial intelligence (AI) or algorithmic component and no relevance to clinical reproductive medicine or AI beats. It is well outside the scope of this digest.
